# Bariatric Surgery Preoperative Assessment(Archived)

**Authors:** Anna R. Sall, Mark W. Jones

**Source:** StatPearls - StatPearls Publishing

## Abstract

Obesity is an ever-growing concern throughout the world. In the last 3 decades, obesity has risen by 27.5% for adults and 47.1% for children internationally. In the United States, the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) recorded the prevalence of obesity in adolescents at 18.5% and in adults at 39.6% from 2015 to 2016.  Individuals with obesity have a higher prevalence of chronic health conditions such as hypertension, osteoarthritis, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease, as well as increased surgical complications and overall mortality. Dietary modification and increased physical activity are the initial management strategies for obesity. Guidelines for nonoperative obesity management are designed to assist patients in achieving clinically significant weight loss, defined as a weight loss of at least 5% of their initial body weight. Multiple diets have demonstrated potential for weight loss, and choosing a diet with the best chance of patient compliance is recommended. To achieve and sustain significant results, the guidelines recommend 14 counseling sessions that target the behavioral aspects of obesity during the first 6 months of attempted weight loss, with regular follow-up appointments thereafter. Increasing physical activity also promotes weight loss. However, guidelines and a better understanding of the physiology and psychology of obesity are sometimes not enough. Weight loss surgery has recently become an additional option to help patients achieve significant and sustainable weight loss. With surgical advances and an improved understanding of the mechanisms of weight loss surgery, surgical management of severe obesity and metabolic disorders provides significant benefits for individuals struggling with obesity.  An essential step in weight loss surgery is the preoperative assessment. The preoperative assessment employs an in-depth, multidisciplinary approach to identify patients who qualify for weight loss surgery and are likely to benefit from one of the recognized procedures. Weight loss surgery is not to be undertaken lightly. There are preoperative barriers to negotiate and postoperative guidelines to follow. Patients undergoing weight loss surgery require extensive education during the preoperative period to facilitate a thorough understanding of the procedure and improve postoperative outcomes.
